FACTUAL BACKGROUND
2
The Oakland Unified School District ("OUSD" or "District") is located in Oakland,
3
California and serves nearly 34,000 students and employs more than 3,000 educators in 84
4
schools consisting of 51 elementary schools, 11 middle schools, 11 high schools, 6 alternative
5
schools and 24 charter schools in addition to preschool programs, a Young Adult Program and a
6
7 Home to Hospital Program that serves students with a temporary illness or injury that makes
8
attending school impossible or inadvisable. Oakland, California draws students from a diverse
9
socio economic, ethnic, and linguistic background. Approximately 18% of the District students
in TK-12 are students with disabilities who receive special education services.
11
The District is a public school employer within the meaning of Section 3540.1 (k) of the
12
13 Educational Employment Relations Act ("EERA"). The Oakland Education Association
14
("OEA" or ''Association'') is the recognized employee organization within the meaning of
15
Section 3540.1 of the EERA and has been the duly recognized representative of 3000
16
certificated non-management members of the bargaining unit.
17
The parties' efforts to negotiate a successor collective bargaining agreement ended in
19 impasse after fifteen negotiating sessions. On November 6, 2025. The Association filed a
20
Request for Impasse Detem1ination and on November 14, 2025, PERB determined impasse
21
existed and assigned a mediator. On December 17, 2025, PERB released the parties to Fact
22
Finding and PERB appointed Cheryl Stevens as the neutral Fact Finder on January 20, 2025.
A. Financial Data
24
25 The evidence presented by the pat1ies is in dispute as to whether the District has the
26
financial means to pay the Association's proposed wage increase and other proposed contract
27
changes. The Association contends that it was unable to fully assess the District's financial
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17. 2026-4

situation because it did not receive clear data and the information was constantly evolving,
2
making it difficult for the Association to determine exactly how much the District has available
3
to spend on wages and OEA's other demands.
4
The District explained that a 1% salary increase represents $2,747,000 for Association
5
members and $5,043,000 for all District employees. (District Exh. 1) The District reported more
6
7 than $837 million in operating revenues for 2024-2025. (District Exh. 4) Yet the ongoing
8
declining enrollment has significantly impacted the revenue it receives from the State. In fact,
9
the District's LCFF revenue did not increase with the COLA and as a result the District incutTed
10
significant deficit spending in 2024-2025 and the District's reserves declined significantly in
I I
2024-2025. Specifically, the District's LCFF revenues decreased by more than $9.4 million or
12
13 1.94% and was the primary reason there was no wage increase in 2024-2025. (District Exh. 8)
14
While there was significant decline in revenue, expenditures exceeded revenues by $61 million
15
requiring the District to spend 52% of its reserves in 2024-2025 and continued reduction in
16
revenues is expected for 2025-2026. (District Exh. 9) Although the Disu·ict was unable to fund
17
a wage increase in 2024-2025 based on the significant reduction in revenue, it still ranks fourth
18
19 among the comparative districts on personnel costs. (District Exh. 11) The District also ranks
20
fifth among the twenty (20) comparative districts on spending for Special Education,
21
representing 14.83% of its total expenses. (District Exh. 14)
22
The State requires school districts to maintain a minimum balance of 3 % of unrestricted
23
reserves. In 2023-2024, the District maintained a balance 13% compared to other unified district
24
25 in the State that maintained an average of 24.36 %. However, the District only maintained a
26
balance of 6.28% in 2024-2025. (District Exhs. 16 and 17) The District has $55,845,233 in
27
unrestricted reserves but $200,777,711 in restricted reserves and the District is prohibited from
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 -5

tapping into the unrestricted reserves to fund the contract changes. Moreover, the District
2
currently has a budget ce11ification status of ''qualified" that is contingent on the District's ability
3
to make significant budget cuts while avoiding new expenditure commitments. For that reason,
4
the District was reluctant to over commit its reserves or agree to increases that would be
5
inconsistent with the limits imposed on their qualified status.
6
7 B. Wage and Benefit Comparison
8
Another statuto1y criteria to consider is a comparison of the wages, hours and conditions
9
of employment of the employees involved in this Factfinding compared to the wages, hours, and
IO
conditions of employment of employees working in comparable positions and comparable
II
communities. OEA presented exhibits that compared their wages with ten other unified school
12
13 districts in the Bay Arca. Based on OEA 's comparison charts, their members are lowest paid
14
educators in the Bay Area. (OEA Exh. l) The District on the other hand relied on twenty
15
districts including the same ten districts in the Association's list of comparable districts;
16
hO\:vevcr, because many of the districts included in the District's list include school districts with
17
lower ADA and as a result Oakland ranks higher. Additionally, the District did not prepare a
18
19 direct comparison of wages; but instead compared salary and benefits per ADA as well as
20
Special Education Expense per ADA. (District Exh. 11, 12 and 14) This comparison places
21
Oakland at the top of the rankings but is not a true comparison of the wages paid to the
22
educators. Furthennore, including ten otherdistricts dilutes the findings improves OUSD's
23
financial profile. Accordingly, I think the Association's reliance on the ten neighboring unified
24
25 school districts for comparison purposes is a more accurate and appropriate comparison.

C. Non-Wage Related Issues
27
There were several non-wage related issues that were raised and discussed in detail on
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 -6

the second day of Fact Finding. Principle among these issues were a commitment to supporting
2
the Visual and Perfonning At1s program, incorporating the Community Schools program into the
3
collective bargaining agreement, addressing safety concerns associated with the demands of the
4
Continuation Schools, modifying class size in grade K-3rd grade and identifying adjustments to
5
the approach of consolidating staff associated with the Newcomers program. The Panel
6
7 recognizes that while these issues are not wage related, they are also not cost neutral, and efforts
8
have been made in this Recommendation to consider these proposals and their associated costs
9
along with the demand for wage increases to establish some balance between all of the
IO
competing factors on the District's budget.
II
For example, the Association believes that reducing class size at the Kindergarten and
12
13 first grade levels will have a positive impact on increasing Oakland's literacy rate even if it
14
results in a slight increase in class size for grades 2 and 3 so long as class sizes for K-3 are able
15
to main ta in the average State required ratio. The District contends that if the class sizes arc
16
reduced in this way, some students will be denied access to their neighborhood or prefetTed
17
schools and will eventually relocate to charter schools or another district thus further reducing
18
19 the decline in enrollment. Although the District's concern might occur, there is no dispute that
20
20 students in a Kindergat1en or first grade class is better than 29 students creating a more
21
conducive learning environment that surely open doors for these students through literacy and
22
establish a stronger foundation. The benefits appear to outweigh the possible loss of revenue;
23
therefore, the Panel recommends reducing class size for K-1s t grade to 22 students.
24
25 As for other non-wage related issues, the parties were able to agree on a definition for
26
Continuation schools and that the administration will notify the sites of any issues with a student
27
prior to placement. OEA wanted a cap of 25 on class size for Continuation schools but this did
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 -7

not appear to be a real problem necessitating this change at this time as the classes are usually
2
well below this cap.
3
Additionally, the parties were able to reach agreement regarding some of the issues
4
associated with the Newcomer program, a program that works diligently to provide support to
5
non-English speaking students navigating through the school system. Although the eight-year
6
7 program has identified many competent educators committed to assisting this important
8
population, declining enrollment has triggered transfer and consolidation issues for these
9
educators. OEA seeks to supp01i this program and the educators associated with it and asked
10
that they be given priority in hiring. The District properly recognized that this request is at odds
11
with established hiring procedures based on seniority and other bargained for procedures.
12
13 Therefore, the District's decision to reject this request was reasonable. However, the District
14
agreed to add that either party could request to meet and confer over the impact of the
15
implementation of consolidation.
16
Finally, there were several non-wage related requests made for the Visual and Performin
17
Arts program. Chief among them included advance notice of budget allocation, identifying
18
19 appropriate space for the VA PA classes and identifying a designated space to store equipment
20
and materials. OEA also asked that the TSAs assigned to V APA become codified positions
21
recognized in the CBA because the V APA educators believe their support to be invaluable to the
22
program. While not directly a wage-related request, incorporating the two (2) TSA positions int
23
the CBA creates a strain on the budget. First, it adds 2 positions to the budget and treats these
24
25 TSAs differently from other TSAs in the District. Second, instead of investing resources in the
26
educators who have direct student involvement it diverts important and necessmy resources awa
27
from the students. The District's explanation for not codifying the VAPA positions was
28
HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 - 8

reasonable and otherwise did not indicate these positions would be eliminated. Finally, the
2
District agreed to identitYing space for equipment and materials and working with the V APA
3
educators to identify appropriate performance space in an effort to demonstrate its support of this
4
very important educational tool.

DISCUSSION AND RECOMMENDATION
6
7 It is the role of the Panel to apply the relevant factors set f 011h in EERA, to the facts
8
underlying the impasse presented, and render its best recommendation considering those factors.
9
The factors that apply are discussed herein.

A. The Interests and Welfare of the Public and the Financial Ability of the Public
School
12
13 The parties disagree on whether the Association's proposed wage increase is in the
14
best interest and welfare for the conununity. The Association argues that the District's proposed
15
wages are not competitive; and when compared to the other ten neighboring districts, OEA
16
members arc at the bottom of the salary scale. The Association insists that if the District stopped
17
hiring outside consultants to perform bargaining unit and reduced the wage increases for
18
19 administrators there would be sufficient funds available in the budget to support a wage increase
20
for the educators. Furthem1ore, it is OEA 's position that a significant wage increase is necessary
21
not only to provide the teachers with a comparable wage but also to ensure Oakland students
22
receive the best education based on the quality of the teaching staff recruited and retained
23
because of the District offering competitive sala1ies.
24
25 Fmthermore, OEA reported that increasing salaries would minimize Oakland's high
26
attrition rate and reverse the ten-year trend of 400 educators leaving the District every year.
27
Although the true status of the District's current financial position is unclear, OEA believes that
28

despite the lack of transparency, the District has sufficient resources to fund the requested wage

increase. An increase that is necessary because the teachers are struggling to suppo11 their
3
families with their cmTent salaries. The Association maintains that the District can retain

talented educators and make them feel valued by adequately and competitively compensating

them in a way that demonstrates the District is committed to investing in the future of the

7 students by investing in their teaching staff.

At the outset of the Fact Finding on Febrnary 9, 2026, the Association demanded a wage

increase of 13.50% to 14% plus specialty differentials over two years, at the conclusion of the

second day of Fact Finding they otlercd to reduce that demand to 12% to 14% plus specialist

ditlerentials. The District insists this demand is entirely too rich and could send the District into

13 financial receivership. First, the District insists enrollment is declining which directly impacts
14
the revenue it can expect to receive from the State. The District explained that a 1% wage

increase will cost the District $2,747,000 for Association v.rages and $5,043,000 for all
16
employees. (District Exh. 1) Therefore based on the District's available unrestricted reserves
17
($55,845,000) after operating expenses in the amount of $837 million for the 2024-2025 school
18
19 year (District Exh. 17) there simply is not enough to fund the requested wage increases and
20
maintain the required minimum of 3% for unrestricted reserves over the course of the next two
21
years, especially as any ,vage increase for OEA members will trigger similar increases for other
22
District employees at a rate of $5 million for every 1% . The District insisted employee
23
compensation increases have historically exceeded both COLA and CPI; however, the LCFF
24
25 revenues have not increased with COLA. (District Exh. 8) The District is in a difficult situation
26
because it receives less funding per student because of the declining enrollment, yet the
27
operating expenses continue to increase, and there are insufficient reserves to bridge the gap.

Notwithstanding the challenge for the District to offer wage increases this year, before the
2
second day of Fact Finding the District proposed a 2.5% increase effective June 30, 2026,

another 2% increase for tiers 1-23 and 3 .5% for the top tier effective March 1, 2027, another 2%

effective June 30, 2027 plus an additional $5 million one-time bonus to be paid to all staff on or

before June 30, 2027. The District also considered increasing the percentage if OEA was willing

7 to push payment out past 2027 in the form of a reopener. Both pai1ies considered ways delayed

payment could be accomplished but concluded it was not possible to schedule wage increases

associated ,vith the cmTent contract that would ultimately not be paid until sometime during the

next contract tenn.

While there is certainly merit to each side's claims, the proposed ongoing 14% increase

13 OEA demands exceeds the COLA and CPI and the 6.5%-8% wage increase the District proposed

before the second day of Fact Finding, will not improve OUSD's standing when compared to the
15
ten neighboring districts OEA identified. (OEA Exh. 1) The comparables relied on by the

the community on multiple levels. Although the District does not expect to receive nevv ongoing
18
19 revenue from the State and it fears it will not be able to meet its financial obligations if they
20
accept the Association's demand of a 14% wage increase, the District must actively and
21
aggressively reduce the contracting out and use more of its reserves to finance a wage increase in
22
excess of its proposed 6.5%-8% wage increase. The Association's demand far exceeds the
23
statutmy COLA of 1.07% and is simply not an option. (District Exh. 30) Although the
24
25 Association's demand of an 14% wage increase for the top tier or even a 12% increase for steps
26
1-23 not including the requested differential benefits would cause the District to operate at a
27
deficit over the next two years, the Association should receive more than a 6.5% increase over
28

the two year contract in order to keep the District's educators competitive and to help them keep
2
up with the rising costs ofliving in the Bay Area. (OEA Exh. 2) Therefore, based on the

financial data introduced during Fact Finding, specifically the January 28, 2026 Financial

Stabilization Implementation Plan, the District has identified additional resources for the 2025-

7 and is reviewing $32 million identified in the School Site Budget Reduction in the 2026-27

budget. Based on these identified potential savings, the Panel proposes a wage increase of 3%

effective July 1, 2025 and another increase of 3% effective July 1, 2026 and a final increase of

Special Education educators on July 1, 2026 seems approp1iate.

13 B. Comparison of the Wages, Hours, and Conditions of Employment of the
Employees with other Employees in Public School Employment in Comparable
14
Communities.
15
16 The District identified twenty (20) districts within thi1ty miles, with an average daily
17
attendance (''ADA") of 8000 or more for comparison and also included districts where OEA
18
members are likely to seek employment. OEA, however, limited its comparisons to other
19
20 unified districts in Alameda County with more than 10,000 ADA or where more than fifty (50)
21 OEA members live. These differences in the selection criteria for comparison made it difficult t
22
truly compare the two proposals based on the wages, hours and employment conditions of the
23
neighboring and similarly situated districts. Depending on which comparisons you accept OEA
24
members are either at the bottom of the comparison charts ( 0 EA Exh. l) or somewhere near the
25
26 top of a larger list of comparable school districts. (District Exh. 11) Regardless of which list of
27 comparable districts one considers there is no dispute the Association members are entitled to a

HEARING DATE: FEBRUARY 10, & 17, 2026 - 12

wage increase at least to respond to the annual COLA increases and with CPI. Moreover, the

only OEA members to receive a salary increase in 2024-2025 were the Early Childhood

educators. Therefore, in order to recruit and retain strong educators for the District, wages

should, at a minimum, cover the annual COLA but ideally include an additional bump due to the

expense ofliving in the Bay Area and establishing wages competitive with sun-ounding districts.

8
the bottom of the scale compared to the salaries received by the educators in the neighboring
9
districts I of Fremont ($117,048), San Francisco ($107,5182 ), and Berkeley ($95,460) compared

to Oakland ($82,716.19). The difference in salaries is significant, and a wage increase is

necessary and appropriate to aggressively recruit and retain competent educators.

13
Although the District insists it cannot sustain more than an 8% increase over the course
14
of two years, plus approximately an additional $5 million in a one-time bonus, the District must

streamline its expenses by reducing and eventually eliminating the contracting out expense and

the most important third party beneficiaries of the wage increase. OEA contends the District has

not been transparent about its financial situation and the Panel Chair agrees that it has been

difficult to fully understand the District's financial position. Therefore, OEA has not been able

to adequately challenge the District's claims because the District has not been fotthcoming with

23 all the financial data. Moreover, historically, the District has told OEA it lacks the resources to
24 pay competitive wages, yet at the eleventh hour, the District has found enough funds to either

would be better spent on providing OEA members with a competitive wage and thus eliminate

11 the hemon-haging of personnel the District experiences every year through attrition.

wages it would not only demonstrate the District's commitment to its educators but that it is also

17 hiring consultants ensures that it will satisfy all State mandated objectives but believes at some

point the District must take steps to reduce its reliance on outside, non-bargaining unit

the District to wean itself of consultants by increasing wages while simultaneously and gradually

23 District repeatedly complained that there were too many employees, yet they spent more than

$316,000 on just one outside consultant in 2024-2025. If the District is spending money on

consultants because they do not have enough employees qualified to handle the positions, then

compensation and streamlining positions will eventually generate more funds for larger wage

increases. The District must start the process of shitting away from consultants and supporting

its existing educators with competitive wage increases but the District must prioritize those

resources and begin the reallocation now. While the Panel is not fully convinced the District has

the Panel believes that the District must take bold steps towards establishing competitive wages

and sound working conditions to make its best efforts now.

The data submitted by the District shows a CPI for the State of 2.40% for 2020-21,
20
21
6.60% for 2021-2022, 5.69% for 2022-2023, 3.36% for 2023-2024 and 2.86% for 2024-2025.
22
(District Exh. 2) The District provided data comparing the salary increases to the COLA and
23
CPI for the same time period. (Id.) According to this chart, the District did not always keep up
24
25 with COLA. In fact, there were no increases at all in 2017-18 and 2024-2025 that clearly
26
contributed to the fact that OUSD wages are lagging behind neighboring school districts even

though there was a 15.84% wage increase in 2023-2024 (Id.) Therefore, the recommended wage

increases of 3% effective July 1, 2025, 3% effective July 1 2026, and 3% for tier 1-23 and 4%

and CPI, while making up for the shortfall in the previous years and thus provide wages that will
